newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan governor quits in constitutional row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan governor quits in constitutional row.

text.p: Taiwan's first elected provincial governor resigned on Tuesday in a widening constitutional row over plans by the island's exiled Republic of China government to dismantle his administration in the name of efficiency.

James Soong, 54, angrily told provincial legislators he had informed long-time ally President Lee Teng-hui of his decision to give up the governorship and his seat in the ruling Nationalist Party's guiding central standing committee.
Soong's resignation came just three days after the Nationalists and main opposition Democratic Progressive Party agreed that all provincial elections should be frozen.

The rivals' pact gave a strong boost to a central government drive to radically pare or even eliminate the Taichung-based provincial government in the name of eliminating redundancy in the many areas where the two huge administrations overlap.
Soong, who was not consulted in the deal but was given the task of dismantling the democratic electoral system that brought him to power, said he would have none of it.

"As the first elected governor of Taiwan I have been asked to handle the matter of freezing provincial government elections," Soong told the provincial assembly in Taichung. "This is emotionally unbearable."
Nationalist Party officials said they would try to dissuade Soong from following through on his resignation.
The controversial streamlining drive is laden with implications for Taiwan's political future -- and its bitter rivalry with the Chinese communist government in Beijing.

After losing a civil war to the communists and taking refuge on Taiwan in 1949, the Nationalists maintained governments for all of China's "communist-occupied" provinces as well as one for Taiwan so they could be ready to retake the mainland.

Though most have been mothballed, two provincial governments still operate -- one for Taiwan itself and a Fukien government for the front-line islands of Matsu and Jinmen, the republic's remaining toehold on what Beijing calls Fujian province.

Taiwan's unification-minded New Party angrily withdrew from a multi-party conference at which the dismantling pact was made, saying that to eliminate the provincial government was tantamount to declaring Taiwan's independence.
Taipei and Beijing both espouse reunification but differ so sharply on terms that they refuse even to discuss them. Taipei insists Beijing adopt democratic reforms like its own.
Beijing so adamantly opposes Taiwan's separation that it reserves the right to use military force to thwart anything it perceives as a declaration of independence.

Opposition politicians and constitutional activists also question whether President Lee and his central government have the right to unilaterally disband a provincial government, saying this might exceed his political powers.

Some argue this should be a matter for Taiwan's national parliament, the Legislative Yuan, while others say it should be left to the largely ceremonial National Assembly, whose main power -- the duty to appoint the president -- died with reforms that led to Taiwan's first popular presidential poll in March.
